title: etbb-july-2024-february-2026-update.pdf — section 425
text:
112. Many words in English do not have exact single-term equivalents in many other languages:
these include words for culturally varying concepts such as “fair”, “reasonable”, “evidence”,
“impartial”, “commitment”, “bias”, “compromise”, “mediation”, “depression”, “opportunity”,
“efficiency”, “liability”. As a result, an interpreter may need to use longer phrases or
sentences to convey the speaker’s full meaning across a cultural divide.

113. Conventions of advocacy, such as tag questions and negative questions, are difficult to
translate linguistically and are likely to be doubly confusing when going through an
interpreter.

114. It is difficult to interpret fine distinctions, and these may be hard for the witness to
understand. Such points need to be stated very clearly and built up slowly.
